paragraphs.heading: What it does
paragraphs.text: Completing the square is a technique from elementary algebra. It rewrites a quadratic polynomial a x² + b x + c in the form a (x − h)² + k, for suitable numbers h and k. Seen in terms of the new quantity x − h, the expression is a quadratic with no linear term. Once (x − h)² is isolated and a square root is taken, a quadratic problem shrinks to a linear one.

paragraphs.heading: Why the name
paragraphs.text: The name comes from a picture. Let x be an unknown length, so x² is the area of a square with side x. The term b/a x is then the area of two identical rectangles, each with sides x and b/(2 a). Add one more square, with side b/(2 a), and the pieces fill out a bigger square whose side is x + b/(2 a).

paragraphs.heading: An old method
paragraphs.text: It is the oldest way of solving general quadratic equations, found on Old Babylonian clay tablets from 1800–1600 BCE. Al-Khwarizmi, a polymath who wrote the early algebra treatise Al-Jabr, used it, formalised it and made it widely known. It is still taught in elementary algebra courses. It is also used to graph quadratic functions, to derive the quadratic formula, and in calculus, for example when evaluating Gaussian integrals or finding Laplace transforms.

paragraphs.heading: How it works
paragraphs.text: It rests on the rule for squaring a sum: (x + p)² = x² + 2 p x + p². In any perfect square of this kind, the coefficient of x is twice p and the constant is p². Take x² + 10 x + 28. It is not a perfect square, because (x + 5)² = x² + 10 x + 25, and 28 is not the square of 5. Still, it can be written as (x + 5)² + 3.

paragraphs.heading: The general recipe
paragraphs.text: For any quadratic x² + b x + c, the square (x + 1/2 b)² has the same first two terms. If the x² term has a coefficient a, you first factor a out and then complete the square on what is left. This lets any quadratic be written as a (x − h)² + k. In general, h = −b/(2 a) and k = c − b²/(4 a).

paragraphs.heading: Reading the graph
paragraphs.text: Every quadratic function draws a parabola as its graph. In the form a (x − h)² + k, the point (h, k) is the vertex: the line x = h is the axis of symmetry, and k is the smallest value of the function, or the largest if a < 0. The reason is a pair of shifts. The parabola for x² has its vertex at the origin; replacing x with x − h moves it right by h, and adding k lifts it up by k.

paragraphs.heading: Solving equations
paragraphs.text: Completing the square can solve any quadratic equation. Take x² + 6 x + 5 = 0: the method leads to x + 3 = −2 or x + 3 = 2, so x = −5 or x = −1. Factoring is reliable only when the roots are rational. Completing the square, by contrast, finds the roots even when they are irrational or complex.
